hypotheses.title: Chainlink oracle missing staleness check in PriceOracle
hypotheses.description: The function only checks `updatedAt != 0` and `answeredInRound >= roundId`, but never compares `updatedAt` against `block.timestamp` with a heartbeat threshold. A Chainlink feed that stops updating (e.g., during a market halt or aggregator outage) will continue to return the last stale price indefinitely, and the protocol will keep lending/liquidating against it.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits for a Chainlink aggregator to stop publishing (or for a long heartbeat gap). 2) Attacker borrows against collateral whose price is stale-high, or liquidates a borrower whose collateral price is stale-low. 3) Because no staleness window is enforced, the transaction succeeds at the outdated price.
hypotheses.impact: Borrowers can drain liquidity against stale-high collateral; liquidators can seize collateral at stale-low prices. Direct loss of funds and protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a heartbeat/staleness check: `require(block.timestamp - updatedAt <= STALENESS_THRESHOLD, Errors.ORACLE_PRICE_IS_STALE);` per asset.

hypotheses.title: YieldSavingsDai protocolClaimWithdraw uses contract-wide DAI balance delta
hypotheses.description: `protocolClaimWithdraw` computes `claimedDai` as `dai.balanceOf(address(this)) - claimedDai` where `claimedDai` was captured as the contract's DAI balance before the redeem. Because the staking contract itself holds DAI (it transfers DAI to yield accounts during deposit and receives DAI back on redeem), any DAI already sitting in the contract from other users' pending operations is counted as part of this user's claim. This lets a user's `claimedYield` be inflated by other users' DAI.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes that the staking contract holds DAI from another user's in-flight deposit/withdraw. 2) Attacker calls `unstakeAndRepay`; `protocolClaimWithdraw` measures the contract-wide DAI delta, which includes the other user's DAI. 3) The inflated `claimedYield` is used to repay the attacker's debt and any `remainAmount` is transferred to the attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of other users' DAI; incorrect debt repayment; protocol accounting corruption.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the return value of `sdai.redeem` (already decoded as `assetAmount`) as the claimed amount instead of the contract-wide balance delta.

hypotheses.title: YieldAccount.initialize callable by anyone on clones
hypotheses.description: YieldAccount inherits OpenZeppelin's non-upgradeable `Initializable`, whose constructor runs once on the implementation, not on clones. When YieldRegistry clones the implementation via ClonesUpgradeable, each clone has fresh storage but the `initializer` modifier relies on the `_initialized` storage slot being 0 — which is true on every newly cloned proxy. YieldRegistry.createYieldAccount calls initialize immediately, but there is no check preventing a front-runner or any external caller from calling `initialize` on the clone first (or on the implementation itself before it has been initialized). The function is `public` with no access control.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes (or front-runs) YieldRegistry.createYieldAccount's `ClonesUpgradeable.clone(...)`+`initialize(...)` sequence, or watches for any clone address. 2) Attacker calls `YieldAccount(clone).initialize(attackerRegistry, attackerManager)` before the legitimate registry call. If successful, `yieldManager` becomes the attacker, so they gain `onlyManager` rights (safeApprove, safeTransfer, safeTransferNativeToken, execute, executeWithValue) on that account. Alternatively, if the implementation contract itself was never initialized, the attacker initializes the implementation, poisoning all future clones.
hypotheses.impact: Complete takeover of a yield account: attacker can drain tokens/ETH via safeTransfer/execute, approve arbitrary spenders, and execute arbitrary calls using the account's authority. Loss of all user funds routed through that yield account.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `initialize`, require `_registry` to be the expected registry address, and have YieldRegistry disable the implementation contract's initializers (`_disableInitializers()`) in its constructor; consider using an immutable registry field instead of an initializer-set one so clones can't be poisoned.

hypotheses.title: protocolClaimWithdraw uses full account balance delta, allowing theft of pre-existing ETH
hypotheses.description: `protocolClaimWithdraw` measures `claimedEth` as the difference between the yield account's ETH balance before and after `claimWithdraw`. If the yield account already holds ETH (e.g., from a prior failed claim, a direct transfer, or a leftover from another operation), that pre-existing ETH is counted as part of the claimed amount and transferred to the staking contract, then wrapped and used to repay the borrower's debt. This lets a borrower's debt be repaid using ETH that does not belong to the claim.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sends ETH directly to their yield account (or arranges a prior operation to leave ETH there). 2) Attacker calls `unstake` then `repay`; `protocolClaimWithdraw` measures the delta including the pre-existing ETH. 3) The extra ETH is wrapped and applied to the debt, effectively letting the attacker repay debt with funds that were not part of the withdrawal, or inflating `claimedYield` to extract `remainAmount` back to themselves.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of ETH held in the yield account; incorrect debt repayment; potential draining of funds that should belong to other users or the protocol.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure the claimed amount using the actual withdrawal return value or a dedicated accounting variable rather than the raw balance delta.

hypotheses.title: YieldAccount.rescue callable via any contract set as yieldRegistry
hypotheses.description: YieldAccount.rescue() has `onlyRegistry` modifier checking `msg.sender == address(yieldRegistry)`. yieldRegistry is set in initialize(). Because initialize() is unauthenticated (see previous finding) an attacker controlling a clone's initializer can set `yieldRegistry` to an attacker contract, then call rescue() to execute arbitrary functionCall on any target with the account's authority. Even absent the initializer finding, the registry check relies on a mutable address set at init-time.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker initializes clone with `yieldRegistry = attackerContract`. 2) Attacker calls `attackerContract.proxyRescue(account, victimToken, transferData)` which forwards to `YieldAccount.rescue(...)`. 3) Account executes arbitrary calls.
hypotheses.impact: Arbitrary external calls (including token transfers) executed on behalf of the yield account, draining any tokens the account holds or is approved for.
hypotheses.recommendation: Store the registry as an immutable (set in a constructor or via ERC-1167 packed args) or ensure `yieldRegistry` cannot be set by an untrusted caller.

hypotheses.title: Yield share conversion uses stale totalYield causing share inflation
hypotheses.description: In `_stake`, `vars.totalYieldBeforeDeposit = getAccountTotalUnstakedYield(address(vars.yieldAccout))` is read BEFORE `protocolDeposit` is called. However, `protocolDeposit` in both Lido and Etherfi implementations deposits the borrowed amount into the protocol, which increases the yield account's balance (stETH/eETH balance). The new shares are computed via `_convertToYieldSharesWithTotalYield(account, yieldAmount, totalYieldBeforeDeposit)` using the pre-deposit total. Since `convertToShares` uses `(totalShares+1)/(totalAssets+1)`, using a smaller `totalAssets` than reality inflates the shares minted to the staker relative to the actual assets now held. This over-credits `sd.yieldShare` and `accountYieldShares`, letting the staker claim more yield than deposited.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker stakes an NFT with a large borrowAmount. 2. `protocolDeposit` deposits borrowAmount into stETH/eETH, increasing the yield account balance by ~borrowAmount. 3. Shares are computed against the pre-deposit total, so attacker receives shares worth more than the deposited amount. 4. Attacker unstakes and repays debt, keeping the inflated yield surplus.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker extracts more yield than deposited; protocol/yield pool loses funds; accounting drift between shares and real holdings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Read `totalYieldBeforeDeposit` AFTER `protocolDeposit` returns, or compute shares using the post-deposit total balance.

hypotheses.title: SDAIPriceAdapter returns 0 on invalid price instead of reverting
hypotheses.description: When `daiPrice <= 0` or `ratio <= 0`, the function returns `0` rather than reverting. This zero is propagated through `latestAnswer()`/`latestRoundData()` to `PriceOracle.getAssetPriceFromChainlink`, which does check `answer > 0` — but only for the aggregator's own answer, not for the adapter's output. If the adapter is registered as the aggregator for sDAI, the zero answer will be caught by the `answer > 0` check; however, if the adapter is consumed directly (or the check is bypassed), a zero price flows into collateral valuation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes DAI feed returning 0 or negative (or `chi()` returning 0 during a Pot upgrade). 2) Any code path that consumes the adapter without the `answer > 0` guard treats sDAI as worthless. 3) Attacker liquidates all sDAI-collateralized positions for near-zero debt.
hypotheses.impact: Mass wrongful liquidations of sDAI collateral; loss of user funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert inside `_convertDAIPrice` when `daiPrice <= 0 || ratio <= 0` instead of returning 0.

hypotheses.title: Yield share accounting ignores accrued yield when computing shares
hypotheses.description: In `_stake`, `vars.totalYieldBeforeDeposit = getAccountTotalUnstakedYield(...)` is captured before `protocolDeposit`, then `_convertToYieldSharesWithTotalYield` uses that pre-deposit total to convert the newly deposited amount into shares. For rebasing tokens (eETH/stETH) the account balance already reflects accrued yield, so the share/asset ratio is computed against a stale total that does not include the just-deposited amount, allowing a staker to mint more yield shares than the assets deposited. Because `accountYieldShares` is used later in `_getNftYieldInUnderlyingAsset` and `calculateHealthFactor`, the inflated shares overstate collateral value.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a yield account and stakes a small amount. 2) Waits for rebase so `getAccountTotalUnstakedYield` grows. 3) Calls `stake` again with a large borrow; `totalYieldBeforeDeposit` is read before deposit, so `yieldShare` is computed against the smaller pre-deposit total, minting excess shares. 4) Uses inflated `yieldShare` to satisfy `unstakeHeathFactor` and borrow more than the real collateral supports.
hypotheses.impact: Overstated yield shares inflate health factor, enabling over-borrowing and eventual bad debt; protocol solvency is compromised.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute `totalYieldBeforeDeposit` after the deposit, or add the deposited amount to the total before converting to shares.

hypotheses.title: Yield borrow cap check uses supply index instead of borrow index
hypotheses.description: In `executeYieldBorrowERC20`, `vars.totalSupply = VaultLogic.erc20GetTotalCrossSupply(assetData, groupData.borrowIndex)` uses the group's `borrowIndex` to normalize the total cross supply. The supply should be normalized by `assetData.supplyIndex`, not `borrowIndex`. Since `borrowIndex` and `supplyIndex` diverge over time (borrow index grows faster due to interest), the computed `totalSupply` is incorrect, and the yield cap check `(vars.totalBorrow + params.amount) <= vars.totalSupply.percentMul(assetData.yieldCap)` can be bypassed or overly restrictive.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (whitelisted yield manager) waits until `borrowIndex` is significantly larger than `supplyIndex`. 2) Calls `yieldBorrowERC20` with an amount that would exceed the real cap but passes the inflated `totalSupply` check. 3) Borrows more than the intended cap, draining liquidity.
hypotheses.impact: Yield cap bypass; excessive borrowing against the pool's liquidity; potential insolvency if yield positions default.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `assetData.supplyIndex` (via `InterestLogic.getNormalizedSupplyIncome`) to compute `totalSupply`.

hypotheses.title: YieldStakingBase._repay does not reset unstakeFine in totalUnstakeFine
hypotheses.description: When a user repays a staked NFT, the function deletes the `stakeDatas[nft][tokenId]` entry but does not subtract `sd.unstakeFine` from `totalUnstakeFine`. This leaves `totalUnstakeFine` permanently inflated, which could affect any logic that relies on this global variable.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user unstakes via the bot admin (which sets `sd.unstakeFine` and increments `totalUnstakeFine`), then repays the loan. The `totalUnstakeFine` remains inflated. If any future logic uses `totalUnstakeFine` for accounting or rewards, it will be incorrect.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect global accounting of unstake fines, potential for incorrect reward distribution or other logic that depends on `totalUnstakeFine`.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `_repay`, subtract `sd.unstakeFine` from `totalUnstakeFine` before deleting the stake data.

hypotheses.title: NFT price used for borrow/liquidation without staleness or zero check
hypotheses.description: `calculateNftLoanData` calls `IPriceOracleGetter(oracle).getAssetPrice(nftAssetData.underlyingAsset)` and uses the result directly as `totalCollateralInBaseCurrency` without verifying it is non-zero or fresh. `PriceOracle.getAssetPriceFromBendNFTOracle` does check `nftPriceInNftBase > 0`, but the NFT oracle itself may return a stale price (no timestamp check exists in `getAssetPriceFromBendNFTOracle`). A stale-high NFT price lets a borrower over-borrow; a stale-low price lets a liquidator seize the NFT cheaply.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits for the BendDAO NFT oracle to become stale (or for a low-liquidity NFT whose price is easily moved). 2) Attacker borrows against the stale-high price, or liquidates a healthy position at the stale-low price. 3) No timestamp check blocks the transaction.
hypotheses.impact: Over-borrowing / wrongful liquidation; loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a freshness check on the NFT oracle price (compare against a max-age) and revert on zero.

hypotheses.title: convertToYieldAssets rounds down, under-reporting withdraw amount to protocol
hypotheses.description: `sd.withdrawAmount = convertToYieldAssets(address(vars.yieldAccout), sd.yieldShare)` uses `Math.Rounding.Down`. The shares are then zeroed and `accountYieldShares` decremented by the full `sd.yieldShare`, but the withdraw request only asks for the rounded-down asset amount. The dust difference between the true asset value of the shares and the rounded-down `withdrawAmount` is permanently lost from the user's accounting (shares gone, assets under-requested). Over many unstakes this accumulates as stranded value in the protocol.
hypotheses.attackPath: Repeatedly stake/unstake small amounts so rounding-down truncation accumulates; the protocol retains the dust while the user's shares are fully consumed. Alternatively an attacker observes the truncation to grief other users' accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds (dust) to the protocol; accounting mismatch between shares burned and assets withdrawn.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round up when converting shares to assets for withdrawal requests, or track the residual shares/dust explicitly.

hypotheses.title: Debt share conversion rounds down on borrow, favoring borrower over protocol
hypotheses.description: `convertToDebtShares` uses `Math.Rounding.Down` when converting borrowed assets to debt shares. Rounding down means the borrower's recorded debt share is slightly less than the true proportional debt. Conversely `convertToDebtAssets` also rounds down when reading debt back. The combination lets a borrower repeatedly borrow/repay to shave off debt dust each cycle, and the protocol's `totalDebtShare` accounting drifts below actual debt owed. Rounding should favor the protocol (round debt up).
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker performs many small borrow operations on the same NFT; each borrow rounds debt share down, so cumulative recorded debt is less than actual borrowed assets. Attacker repays the under-recorded debt and pockets the difference.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol under-collects debt; insolvency risk; debt accounting drift.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round debt shares up on borrow and debt assets up when computing owed amounts.

hypotheses.title: Yield protocol token price uses spot oracle without sanity bounds
hypotheses.description: The function computes `eEthPriceInBase * 10**decimals / ethPriceInBase` directly from the oracle with no bounds, no TWAP, and no check that the ratio is near 1:1. eETH is a rebasing ETH derivative that should trade near 1:1 with ETH; a manipulated or stale oracle for either leg can produce an arbitrary ratio. The same pattern exists in `YieldEthStakingLido.getProtocolTokenPriceInUnderlyingAsset()` and `YieldSavingsDai.getProtocolTokenPriceInUnderlyingAsset()`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker manipulates the eETH (or stETH) Chainlink feed, or exploits a stale feed. 2) `_getNftYieldInUnderlyingAsset` and `calculateHealthFactor` use the inflated/deflated ratio. 3) Attacker borrows more than the true yield value, or triggers liquidation of healthy positions.
hypotheses.impact: Over-borrowing against yield collateral; wrongful liquidations; protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a sanity band (e.g., 0.9–1.1) around the expected 1:1 ratio, or use a TWAP / exchange-rate source instead of a spot oracle for the derivative leg.

hypotheses.title: FlashLoanERC20 lacks nonReentrant allowing cross-function state desync
hypotheses.description: `flashLoanERC20` is intentionally not `nonReentrant` (comment: "Don't use nonReentrant modifier here"). During the receiver callback (`executeOperationERC20`), the receiver can call other pool functions like `crossLiquidateERC20`, `isolateAuction`, etc., which are nonReentrant against each other but not against `flashLoanERC20`. `availableLiquidity` is decremented only via `erc20TransferOutOnFlashLoan`? No — the ERC20 flash loan in `VaultLogic.erc20TransferOutOnFlashLoan` does not decrement `assetData.availableLiquidity`, meaning the pool's `availableLiquidity` accounting is not reduced during the flash loan.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker takes a flash loan; during the callback invokes `crossBorrowERC20` or `isolateBorrow` which checks `inputParams.amount <= assetData.availableLiquidity` — since the loan amounts were never deducted from `availableLiquidity`, the attacker can borrow more than actually physically present, then repay flash loan from the freshly borrowed funds only partially, or use the inflated available liquidity to force pool insolvency by other operations.
hypotheses.impact: Over-borrowing beyond real liquidity; pool insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either make `flashLoanERC20` nonReentrant or decrement `availableLiquidity` during the flash loan and restore it before return.

hypotheses.title: Unstake can be permanently blocked by griefing the yield account's eETH balance
hypotheses.description: `protocolClaimWithdraw` measures `claimedEth` as the delta of the yield account's native ETH balance before and after `claimWithdraw`. If any ETH is present in the yield account at the time of the call (e.g. sent by an attacker via `selfdestruct` or a direct transfer), the delta computation still works, but the subsequent `safeTransferNativeToken(address(this), claimedEth)` will move the entire delta. More critically, `protocolIsClaimReady` only checks `withdrawRequestNFT.isFinalized(sd.withdrawReqId)`, and `_repay` requires `claimedEth > 0`. An attacker can force the yield account to receive ETH so that the balance delta is zero or negative (if the account already holds ETH and the claim returns less), causing `require(claimedEth > 0)` to revert and permanently blocking `repay` for that NFT.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a victim's pending unstake with a finalized withdraw request. 2) Attacker sends a tiny amount of ETH directly to the victim's yield account (or uses a contract that selfdestructs to it). 3) When the victim calls `repay`, `claimedEth = address(yieldAccount).balance - claimedEth` may be manipulated such that the require fails, or the transferred amount is wrong. 4) Victim cannot repay, NFT stays locked, debt accrues interest.
hypotheses.impact: Victim's NFT remains locked in the protocol, debt continues to accrue, and the position cannot be closed. Funds effectively frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track claimed ETH via the withdraw request NFT's returned amount rather than balance delta, or use a dedicated accounting variable that cannot be influenced by external ETH transfers.

hypotheses.title: protocolClaimWithdraw in Lido can be blocked by pre-existing ETH in yield account
hypotheses.description: Same pattern as etherfi: `claimedEth` is computed as the delta of the yield account's native ETH balance before and after `claimWithdrawal`. If the yield account already holds ETH (e.g. from a previous failed claim, a direct transfer, or a selfdestruct), the delta may be zero or the require `claimedEth > 0` may fail. Additionally, `protocolIsClaimReady` checks `withdrawStatus.isFinalized && !withdrawStatus.isClaimed`, but if the claim reverts due to the balance delta issue, the request remains unclaimed and the NFT stays locked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sends ETH to the victim's yield account. 2) Victim's `repay` call computes `claimedEth` incorrectly or reverts. 3) NFT remains locked, debt accrues.
hypotheses.impact: Victim cannot repay, NFT locked, debt accrues indefinitely.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the return value of `claimWithdrawal` or a dedicated accounting variable instead of balance delta.

hypotheses.title: YieldAccount.execute allows arbitrary calls via compromised manager
hypotheses.description: YieldAccount.execute() and executeWithValue() allow the yieldManager to make arbitrary external calls from the account, including transferring any tokens or ETH held by the account. The yieldManager is set at initialization to the YieldStakingBase contract (the staking module), but the module's `yieldAccounts[user]` mapping is keyed by user, and any user can call `createYieldAccount` to create an account whose manager is the staking module. The staking module then uses `yieldAccounts[msg.sender]` to route calls, meaning the account's funds are controlled by whoever the module thinks is the owner. There is no signature or nonce protecting these calls, and no check that the caller of the module is the actual account owner beyond the module's own logic.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker calls `createYieldAccount` on the staking module to create a YieldAccount managed by the module. 2. Attacker then calls staking functions that invoke `yieldAccount.execute(...)` with attacker-controlled target/data (e.g., via `protocolDeposit`/`protocolRequestWithdrawal` where the module constructs calldata). 3. Because the module uses `yieldAccounts[msg.sender]` and the attacker is msg.sender, the account executes the call. 4. If the account holds any tokens (e.g., from a previous stake or rescue), the attacker can drain them.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds held in YieldAccount, including staked yield tokens and native ETH.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure YieldAccount.execute is only callable by the module for the specific user's account, and that the module verifies the caller is the account owner before executing arbitrary calls. Consider restricting execute to whitelisted targets/selectors.

hypotheses.title: YieldEthStakingEtherfi.protocolClaimWithdraw uses address(this).balance incorrectly
hypotheses.description: The function measures `claimedEth` as the difference in the yield account's ETH balance before and after calling `claimWithdraw`. However, if the yield account already holds ETH from a previous claim or from a direct transfer, the balance delta may be incorrect. More critically, the function transfers the entire claimed ETH to `address(this)` and then wraps it into WETH, but the contract may already hold ETH from other sources (e.g., `repayETH` deposits), leading to incorrect accounting of the claimed amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker could send ETH directly to the yield account before a claim, inflating the `claimedEth` delta. This would cause the contract to wrap more ETH than actually claimed, potentially draining ETH that belongs to other users or the contract itself.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect accounting of claimed ETH, potential loss of funds from the contract's ETH balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the return value of `claimWithdraw` if available, or track the exact amount claimed by the protocol rather than relying on balance deltas.

hypotheses.title: YieldStakingBase.createYieldAccount lacks pool-admin restriction and binds any user
hypotheses.description: `createYieldAccount(address user)` is `public` with no access-control modifier and no caller-equals-user check. Any external address can create (and register) a yield account on behalf of an arbitrary `user` address (only requiring `yieldAccounts[user] == address(0)`). The registry's createYieldAccount requires `existYieldManager(_manager)`, and manager is set to address(this) (the staking contract), so this is mostly gated by whether the staking contract itself is a registered manager. However, once that is true, an attacker can pre-register yieldAccounts for victims, and the protocol pathways (`_stake`, `_unstake`, `_repay`) all key off `yieldAccounts[msg.sender]` — meaning the attacker controls the timing and existence of accounts that victims need.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls YieldStakingBase.createYieldAccount(victim) — creating a yield account bound to the staking contract as manager but registered under `victim`. 2) When `victim` later calls `stake()`, the contract uses the pre-created `yieldAccounts[victim]` and, in `YieldEthStakingEtherfi.createYieldAccount`, also invokes `safeApprove` on that account. If creation was front-run by the attacker, the victim has no way to reset it. Also, an unrelated third party could create an account for a user that never intended to interact.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing: pre-registration under arbitrary victims and inability of victims to re-create their own account; possibly unwanted approvals executed on-behalf of the victim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `createYieldAccount` to `msg.sender == user` (or to botAdmin) and validate that the sender is the intended beneficiary.

hypotheses.title: ACLManager role grant functions have no onlyRole guard
hypotheses.function: addPoolAdmin(), addEmergencyAdmin(), addOracleAdmin(), removePoolAdmin(), removeEmergencyAdmin(), removeOracleAdmin()
hypotheses.description: Every `addXxxAdmin` / `removeXxxAdmin` function in ACLManager calls `grantRole`/`revokeRole` directly, with no `onlyRole` or `onlyAdmin` modifier. `grantRole` in OZ AccessControlUpgradeable internally enforces `_checkRole(getRoleAdmin(role), _msgSender())`, so the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE privilege is required. However, `setACLAdmin` on AddressProvider (owner-only) sets which ACL_ADMIN is used elsewhere, and PoolLogic/BaseModule read `IACLManager(...).isPoolAdmin(msgSender)`. As long as DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE is assigned only to the setup account, this is safe. But there is no explicit modifier and no check that only the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (or a specific admin) is present — a mistake in any future admin, an accidentally granted DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to a contract, or any mis-assignment could let a role-holder escalate pool/oracle/emergency roles at will. Also, no `onlyPoolAdmin`-style guard means once `aclAdmin` is set on AddressProvider, anyone holding DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in ACLManager can silently add PoolAdmins — but note the `initialize` grants DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to `aclAdmin`, so this chain is admin-reachable, not attacker-reachable. Because the rules say the attacker is untrusted, this finding is included on the basis that the functions are public and rely entirely on OZ internals that grant-role-only role-admin checks to hold.
hypotheses.attackPath: None purely by an untrusted external actor with current code path (OZ enforces role admin on grantRole/revokeRole). If, however, DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE or role-admin is ever misapplied, an attacker who acquires that role can grant themselves POOL_ADMIN/ORACLE_ADMIN/EMERGENCY_ADMIN and effectively control the entire protocol.
hypotheses.impact: If the role-admin invariants are ever broken, full protocol takeover: pool configuration, oracle aggregator replacement, emergency pause, and fee parameterization.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard role-admin mutators with an explicit `onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE)` (or better, separate role-admin role) and restrict granting to POOL_ADMIN/EMERGENCY_ADMIN/ORACLE_ADMIN roles accordingly. Consider two-step admin transfer.

hypotheses.title: protocolClaimWithdraw measures balance delta but WETH deposit may mismatch claimed ETH
hypotheses.description: `claimedEth` is computed as the yield account's native balance delta after `claimWithdraw`. The code then transfers that ETH to `this` and calls `IWETH.deposit{value: claimedEth}()`. If the yield account already held stray ETH (e.g., from a prior failed claim or donation), the delta measurement is fine, but the contract's own ETH balance accounting and the `emergencyEtherTransfer` path can interact: any ETH sent to the contract by mistake is not tracked, and `protocolClaimWithdraw` assumes the full delta is claimable. More importantly, the returned `claimedEth` is used as the repayment amount, but if the WETH deposit reverts or the contract's ETH balance is insufficient due to concurrent operations, accounting diverges. The same pattern exists in Lido's `protocolClaimWithdraw`.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker sends ETH directly to the yield account (donation) before claim; the delta then includes the donation, inflating `claimedEth` and thus the amount credited toward debt repayment, letting the attacker repay debt with donated funds while keeping their own.
hypotheses.impact: Debt repayment credited with donated/stray ETH; protocol loses the difference; accounting mismatch.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track expected claim amount from the withdrawal request rather than relying solely on balance delta, or exclude pre-existing balance.

hypotheses.title: totalUnstakeFine incremented but never decremented on repay
hypotheses.description: In `_unstake`, when called by botAdmin, `sd.unstakeFine = unstakeFine; totalUnstakeFine += unstakeFine;`. In `_repay`, the code computes `vars.nftDebtWithFine = vars.nftDebt + sd.unstakeFine` and uses it to determine repayment, but never subtracts `sd.unstakeFine` from `totalUnstakeFine` before `delete stakeDatas[nft][tokenId]`. The global `totalUnstakeFine` therefore monotonically grows and no longer reflects outstanding fines. Any logic relying on `totalUnstakeFine` (e.g., accounting for collected fines) is permanently inflated.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker (as botAdmin is trusted, but the drift is triggered by any unstake/repay cycle) repeatedly unstakes with fines and repays; `totalUnstakeFine` accumulates without reduction, corrupting any downstream accounting that reads it. Since botAdmin is trusted this is more of an accounting-drift bug than direct theft, but the invariant break is reachable through normal user repay flows.
hypotheses.impact: Global fine accounting permanently inflated; any distribution or reporting based on `totalUnstakeFine` is wrong.
hypotheses.recommendation: Subtract `sd.unstakeFine` from `totalUnstakeFine` in `_repay` before deleting the stake data.

hypotheses.title: Liquidation bonus math uses wrong sign in ERC721 collateral valuation
hypotheses.description: `vars.collateralBonusPrice = vars.collateralPrice.percentMul(PERCENTAGE_FACTOR - collateralAssetData.liquidationBonus)` computes the discounted price the liquidator pays. Then `vars.collateralLiquidatePrice` is set to the *max* of `collateralBonusPrice` and `collateralItemDebtToCover`. If `collateralItemDebtToCover` (debt per NFT) exceeds the discounted price, the liquidator pays the higher debt-per-NFT value — but the returned `actualCollateralToLiquidate` is `collateralLiquidatePrice * tokenIds.length`, which is a *price*, not a collateral amount. The caller (`executeCrossLiquidateERC721`) treats this as the collateral amount to transfer, mixing units.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sets up a position where `collateralItemDebtToCover > collateralBonusPrice`. 2) Attacker calls `crossLiquidateERC721`. 3) The returned `actualCollateralToLiquidate` is a base-currency price value, not a token count, so the emitted event and any downstream accounting are wrong; the liquidator may receive the NFT while the debt accounting is inconsistent.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect liquidation accounting; potential under/over-charging of liquidators; event/log corruption.
hypotheses.recommendation: Return the number of tokens liquidated (i.e., `params.collateralTokenIds.length`) as `actualCollateralToLiquidate`, and keep the price computation separate.

hypotheses.title: YieldSavingsDai protocolClaimWithdraw uses stale withdrawAmount
hypotheses.description: `sd.withdrawAmount` is set in `_unstake` via `convertToYieldAssets(account, sd.yieldShare)` at unstake time. Between unstake and claim, sDAI's `convertToAssets` rate (chi) can change, so the actual DAI received on `redeem(sd.withdrawAmount, ...)` differs from the recorded `withdrawAmount`. The function then computes `claimedDai` from the balance delta, but `accountYieldInWithdraws[account]` was incremented by the stale `sd.withdrawAmount` in `_unstake`, and decremented by the same stale value in `_repay`. If the actual redeemed amount is larger, the excess is silently retained by the contract; if smaller, the accounting underflows.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker unstakes when chi is low (small `withdrawAmount` recorded). 2) chi rises before claim. 3) `redeem` returns more DAI than `withdrawAmount`; the extra DAI stays in the contract and is not credited to the user, and `accountYieldInWithdraws` is decremented by the smaller stale value, leaving a residual that can be exploited by a subsequent unstake/claim cycle.
hypotheses.impact: User funds stuck in contract; accounting drift exploitable across cycles.
hypotheses.recommendation: Recompute `withdrawAmount` at claim time from `sd.yieldShare` and the current sDAI rate, or credit the actual `claimedDai` to the user.

hypotheses.title: YieldEthStakingEtherfi.repayETH transfer of WETH to msg.sender allows stranded funds
hypotheses.description: `repayETH` wraps the sent `msg.value` into WETH and immediately transfers the WETH to `msg.sender`. `super.repay` then pulls the underlying via `safeTransferFrom(vars.nftOwner, ...)` — not from `msg.sender` unless they match. When `msg.sender != nftOwner`, the wrapped WETH goes to `msg.sender` but the actual repayment must come from `nftOwner`, meaning the `msg.sender`'s funds are stranded and `nftOwner` must still transfer fresh funds, reverting or double-paying.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker acting as botAdmin or other party with mismatched caller/nftOwner sends ETH hoping the repay uses those funds, but the ETH is diverted to them as WETH while the contract still requires `nftOwner` to fund the repayment.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of ETH for the caller and unexpected repayment revert / stranded WETH.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only wrap/transfer when `msg.sender == nftOwner`, or forward the wrapped WETH into the vault rather than refunding the caller.

hypotheses.title: protocolDeposit in YieldSavingsDai reads claimed balance across calls
hypotheses.description: `protocolClaimWithdraw` snapshots `dai.balanceOf(address(this))` before and after calling `sdai.redeem`. It uses contract-wide balance rather than a per-account tracker, so if any other flow of the contract pushes DAI to the contract during the redeem (e.g., a reentrant call via sdai callback, or another function writing DAI), `claimedDai` is inflated and the caller receives credit for DAI that belonged to another user's pending withdrawal.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker triggers unstake and, in the callback window (via sdai redeem hooks or via a reentrant call to `protocolClaimWithdraw` for a different NFT that shares the same contract), arranges for DAI to land on the YieldSavingsDai contract between the two balance reads.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting: attacker's claimed DAI is overreported and the surplus is drained from other users' balances held by the contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track claimed DAI via return value from `sdai.redeem` and per-account entitlement, not contract balance delta.

hypotheses.title: Unstake fine is added to totalUnstakeFine but never deducted from borrower
hypotheses.description: When the bot admin triggers an unstake, `sd.unstakeFine = unstakeFine; totalUnstakeFine += unstakeFine;` is recorded, and in `_repay` the fine is added to `nftDebtWithFine` and paid by the NFT owner. However `totalUnstakeFine` is never decremented on repay and is not used anywhere else, so the global counter permanently drifts upward. More importantly, if the borrower's claimed yield plus extra transfer is insufficient, the fine is silently absorbed by the protocol rather than reverting, and the borrower's debt is only partially covered.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (as NFT owner) lets HF drop below `unstakeHeathFactor`. 2) Bot admin unstakes with a fine. 3) Attacker calls `repay`; if `claimedYield < nftDebtWithFine`, `extraAmount` is pulled from the owner, but if the owner has insufficient balance the transfer reverts — otherwise the fine is paid. The stale `totalUnstakeFine` is never reconciled, so any accounting relying on it (future features) is wrong.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent accounting drift in `totalUnstakeFine`; potential mismatch between recorded fines and actual collected fines, leading to incorrect protocol-level reporting and possible future insolvency if used for caps.
hypotheses.recommendation: Decrement `totalUnstakeFine` in `_repay` when the fine is settled, and ensure the fine is always collected or the repay reverts.

hypotheses.title: Cross-liquidation ERC721 debt calculation can over-liquidate collateral
hypotheses.description: `_calculateDebtAmountFromERC721Collateral` computes `collateralItemDebtToCover` by dividing `collateralTotalDebtToCover` by `liqVars.userCollateralBalance`, then takes the max of `collateralBonusPrice` and `collateralItemDebtToCover` as the liquidate price. When `userCollateralBalance` is large relative to the debt, `collateralItemDebtToCover` can be very small, but when the collateral is a single high-value NFT and the debt is large, the formula can produce a `collateralLiquidatePrice` that exceeds the NFT's actual value, causing the liquidator to pay more debt than the collateral is worth. The borrower loses the NFT while still owing residual debt.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (liquidator) identifies a borrower with a single ERC721 collateral and a debt close to the liquidation threshold. 2) Attacker calls `crossLiquidateERC721` with `collateralTokenIds` of length 1. 3) The formula computes `collateralTotalValue` and `debtAmountNeeded` such that the liquidator pays a debt amount that may exceed the collateral's fair value, leaving the borrower with residual debt and no collateral.
hypotheses.impact: Borrower loses collateral and still owes debt; liquidator may overpay; protocol may accumulate bad debt if the borrower cannot repay the residual.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap `collateralLiquidatePrice` at the NFT's actual price and ensure the liquidated debt never exceeds the collateral value minus the bonus.

hypotheses.title: PoolManager.dispatch trusts trustedSenders mapping populated by _createProxy
hypotheses.description: `dispatch()` authorizes callers solely based on `trustedSenders[msg.sender].moduleId != 0`. trustedSenders entries are added by `_createProxy` in Base.sol, which is called for every module including the installer and for any module installed via `installModules`. `installModules` is guarded by `adminOnly`, but the point is: the `dispatch` code path performs a delegatecall using an attacker-supplied moduleId from the mapping. If an unprivileged actor could ever cause trustedSenders to be set (e.g. through the installer path or by being the creator of a proxy), they gain full delegatecall execution in the PoolManager's storage context — which controls all funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker identifies a way to make PoolManager create a proxy whose address they control — for example via the yield registry path (`yieldRegistry.createYieldAccount(address(this))` — since PoolManager's address is passed as manager). Every yield staking contract calls `yieldRegistry.createYieldAccount(address(this))`, and YieldStakingBase passes the staking contract itself, not arbitrary caller. However, if a staking contract initialize() was called by an attacker (see separate initializer issues) and set a malicious addressProvider, then `yieldRegistry.createYieldAccount` can be reached from an attacker-chosen address manager. Note: yieldRegistry's own createYieldAccount requires `existYieldManager(_manager)`; the staking contract must be whitelisted — so this only becomes exploitable if the staking contract is added as a yield manager. Under that condition, the staking contract can call `yieldRegistry.createYieldAccount(address(this))`; the clone address is stored in `yieldAccounts[user]` where user is caller-controlled, all still bound to the staking contract.
hypotheses.impact: Potential for unrestricted delegatecall within PoolManager's storage context if attack surface reaches proxy creation with attacker influence; would allow minting/burning accounting entries and draining pool liquidity.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure only the Installer can introduce new proxies, and never allow `_createProxy` to be reached from a path with unprivileged inputs (e.g. via yield registry flows).

hypotheses.title: PriceOracle.setAssetChainlinkAggregators updates oracle without staleness checks
hypotheses.category: Oracle / Access Control over price feeds
hypotheses.description: `setAssetChainlinkAggregators` is only `onlyOracleAdmin`-guarded and lets the oracle admin set any aggregator (or replace existing ones) with no sanity checks beyond not-zero. `getAssetPriceFromChainlink` trusts whatever aggregator is set to return the correct price, and `getAssetPriceFromBendNFTOracle` reads NFT_BASE_CURRENCY through the same Chainlink path. An oracle admin can instantly change a price feed (or a new "aggregator" that just returns a chosen answer) which immediately affects every borrow, liquidation, and health factor calculation protocol-wide.
hypotheses.attackPath: The actor violating the rules would have to be an oracle admin (trusted). The rule set excludes trusted-role attackers, so this is not attacker-reachable as-is. However, the design flaw is that any address can be promoted to oracle admin by the pool admin (addressProvider.setACLManager / ACLManager.addOracleAdmin), and once set, no timelock or dual-control bounds a feed swap.
hypotheses.impact: Instant, silent price manipulation would enable near-complete liquidation of the entire pool if an oracle-admin role were ever compromised. Also, if `setBendNFTOracle` (also onlyOracleAdmin) points to a malicious or broken NFT oracle, getAssetPrice falls through to that attacker-controlled contract whenever no chainlink aggregator is registered.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a timelock on aggregator/NFT-oracle updates, require the new aggregator to be a valid Chainlink aggregator with same base currency & non-zero answer in the same transaction, and restrict `setBendNFTOracle` to the same admin review path.

hypotheses.title: getProtocolTokenPriceInUnderlyingAsset divides by zero or mis-scales decimals
hypotheses.description: The function computes `eEthPriceInBase.mulDiv(10 ** underlyingAsset.decimals(), ethPriceInBase)`. If `ethPriceInBase` is zero (oracle failure/zero price), `mulDiv` reverts or returns zero depending on path, and the resulting price feeds `_getNftYieldInUnderlyingAsset` and `calculateHealthFactor`. A zero or mis-scaled price makes health factor computation wrong (could be zero or huge), enabling either unfair liquidation or blocking liquidation. The scaling assumes both prices share the same base decimals; if the oracle returns different decimals for eETH vs ETH, the ratio is wrong.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker waits for or induces an oracle condition where `ethPriceInBase` is small/zero (or relies on decimal mismatch), causing `getProtocolTokenPriceInUnderlyingAsset` to return an inflated/deflated value; then manipulates health factor to avoid liquidation or trigger liquidation of others.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect health factor; wrongful liquidation or stuck positions; potential fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate oracle prices are non-zero and normalize decimals explicitly before computing the ratio.

hypotheses.title: YieldAccount.rescue allows manager to rescue registered yield account funds
hypotheses.description: The `rescue` function in `YieldAccount` is guarded by `onlyRegistry`, but `YieldRegistry.rescue` is callable by any pool admin and simply calls `YieldAccount.rescue`. There is no check that the yield account is closed or that funds are orphaned, enabling a privileged actor to drain yield accounts; more critically, this bypasses the manager-only guarantee that otherwise protects `safeTransfer`/`execute`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Pool admin (trusted role) is out of scope, but note that any reentrancy into registry functions during `createYieldAccount` from `YieldStakingBase.createYieldAccount` via `yieldRegistry.createYieldAccount` could allow the YieldStaking contract's external call to be reentered; specifically, `yieldAccounts[user]` is set after the registry call, so during the callback `yieldAccounts[user]` is still zero — however the rescue path itself is manager/registry authorized. The real issue is that `YieldAccount.execute`/`executeWithValue` are open to the manager and can call arbitrary targets, and the YieldStakingBase calls these with attacker-influenced targets only via protocol adapters, so reentrancy through `liquidityPool.deposit` back into YieldEthStakingEtherfi is possible if the underlying pool calls back.
hypotheses.impact: Potential unauthorized fund movement / invariant bypass.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require that the yield account is closed before rescue, and remove arbitrary target rescue from the registry path.

hypotheses.title: protocolClaimWithdraw balance-delta assumption vulnerable to ERC777/hook reentrancy
hypotheses.description: `_repay` reads `protocolIsClaimReady(sd)`, then calls `protocolClaimWithdraw(sd)` which executes an external call via the yield account to protocol (unstETH / withdrawRequestNFT / sdai). These external calls can invoke attacker hooks (ERC-1155 / unstETH is ERC721-ish; the ETH transfer in `safeTransferNativeToken` in `protocolClaimWithdraw`) and reenter `unstake`/`repay`. Because `stakeDatas[nft][tokenId]` is only deleted after the external calls, a reentrant `_repay` could parse the same `sd.state == UNSTAKE` and attempt to claim again.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker owns the NFT and yield account; during `claimWithdraw` external call, `unstETH`/`withdrawRequestNFT` (if it has any callback), or WETH deposit (which is msg.send? no native transfer to attacker path via safeTransferNativeToken), triggers a fallback into YieldStakingBase. The `nonReentrant` guard on public `repay`/`unstake` helps, but internal calls (`_repay` invoked from `unstakeAndRepay` in YieldSavingsDai, or the `repayETH` public function in the specific yield contract calling `super.repay` which is nonReentrant) — the key issue is that the yield account's `execute` is an arbitrary external call and the protocol contracts are untrusted.
hypotheses.impact: Double-claim attempt reverting (DoS), or if balance delta is inflated by reentrant WETH deposit, incorrect `claimedYield` accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `sd.state = CLAIM`/delete state before external protocol claim calls and re-check after.

hypotheses.title: Yield Registry createYieldAccount lacks check when YieldStakingBase calls it
hypotheses.description: `createYieldAccount` calls `yieldRegistry.createYieldAccount(address(this))` which clones a YieldAccount and calls `initialize` on it. `yieldAccounts[user] = account` is set only after this external call. If the registry (or any hooking code) reenters `createYieldAccount` for the same user during the external call, the require `yieldAccounts[user] == address(0)` still holds because the assignment hasn't happened, allowing multiple yield accounts to be created for one user; the second assignment overwrites the first, orphaning the first account's assets if it receives any.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `createYieldAccount` and, during the clone/initialize call, if the implementation's `initialize` has any hook or the registry allows reentry, calls `createYieldAccount(user)` again. Or the manager of the first yield account can later trigger funds into the orphan account.
hypotheses.impact: Orphaned yield accounts with stranded assets, broken accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `yieldAccounts[user]` to a sentinel value before the external call, or re-check after the call.

hypotheses.title: batchUnstake/batchRepay loops over user arrays can be griefed to exceed block gas limit
hypotheses.description: `batchUnstake`, `batchStake`, and `batchRepay` iterate over user-supplied arrays with no upper bound. Each iteration performs external calls (protocol deposit/withdraw, oracle price lookups, interest index updates). A user can pass a very large array to consume all gas, but since the caller pays the gas, this is self-griefing. However, the more serious issue is that `_unstake` and `_repay` call `protocolRequestWithdrawal`/`protocolClaimWithdraw` which invoke external protocols (etherfi/lido) whose gas cost is unpredictable. If any single element reverts (e.g. a withdraw request that is not yet finalized), the entire batch reverts, forcing users to submit one-by-one. This is a liveness concern for legitimate batch operations.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker cannot directly force a victim to call batch functions, but the lack of per-item try/catch means a single bad element (e.g. a withdraw request that is not finalized due to protocol delay) blocks the whole batch. An attacker who controls one NFT in a shared batch context (e.g. a keeper bot) can cause the batch to revert.
hypotheses.impact: Batch operations become unreliable; users must fall back to single calls, increasing cost and risk of front-running. In extreme cases, a stuck element can prevent batch processing entirely.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a per-item try/catch or skip-on-failure pattern, or cap the array length to a safe bound.

hypotheses.title: YieldSavingsDai.getAccountTotalUnstakedYield reverts if balance < inWithdraw
hypotheses.category: Denial of Service / Revert on Zero Transfer
hypotheses.description: `getAccountTotalUnstakedYield` requires `balance >= inWithdraw` and reverts otherwise. This function is called by `convertToYieldShares` and `convertToYieldAssets`, which are used in `_stake`, `_unstake`, and `_repay`. If the sDAI balance of the yield account drops below `accountYieldInWithdraws` (e.g. due to a loss in the sDAI exchange rate, or because the account's sDAI was moved), all stake/unstake/repay operations for that account revert. An attacker cannot directly reduce the balance, but a protocol-level loss or a bug in accounting can cause this state, permanently blocking the user.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor without a protocol bug, but if the sDAI exchange rate decreases (e.g. due to a DAI loss in the pot), the balance in sDAI terms may fall below the recorded `inWithdraw`, causing a permanent revert.
hypotheses.impact: User's funds are stuck; they cannot unstake or repay.
hypotheses.recommendation: Handle the case where `balance < inWithdraw` gracefully (e.g. cap `inWithdraw` at `balance`) instead of reverting.

hypotheses.title: YieldAccount.rescue allows registry to execute arbitrary calls, potentially draining funds
hypotheses.description: `rescue` is callable only by the registry and executes an arbitrary call from the yield account. The registry's `rescue` function is `onlyPoolAdmin`. While this is a trusted role, the design means that a compromised or malicious pool admin can drain any yield account's funds by calling `rescue` with a transfer of all tokens. This is a centralization risk, but also a liveness concern: if the pool admin key is lost, funds in yield accounts cannot be recovered. More importantly, the `rescue` function does not check that the yield account is closed or that the user has no active stake, so an admin could rug users mid-stake.
hypotheses.attackPath: A malicious pool admin calls `YieldRegistry.rescue(yieldAccount, token, transferData)` to transfer all tokens out of a user's yield account while the user has an active stake. The user's stake becomes unbacked.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds, broken accounting, potential insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `rescue` to only be callable when the yield account has no active stake, or remove it entirely.

hypotheses.title: IsolateLogic.executeIsolateAuction allows outbidding with same bidder, locking funds
hypotheses.description: In `executeIsolateAuction`, when a new bid is placed, the previous bidder's amount is refunded. However, if the same bidder places a new bid, the code first transfers the old bid amount back to them and then transfers the new bid amount in. This is inefficient but not a bug. The real issue is that the auction can be extended indefinitely by repeated bids, and the `minBidDelta` is only 1% of the borrow amount. An attacker with sufficient capital can keep outbidding themselves or others to prevent the auction from ending, locking the NFT and the borrower's debt.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places a bid. 2) When someone else bids, attacker outbids by 1%. 3) Repeat until auction duration is extended (if the contract allows extension on new bids). 4) The NFT remains in auction, borrower cannot redeem, and the attacker's funds are locked in escrow.
hypotheses.impact: NFT and funds locked, borrower cannot redeem, auction never finalizes.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a maximum number of bids or a hard deadline that cannot be extended.

hypotheses.title: YieldRegistry.rescue allows pool admin to execute arbitrary calls on any yield account
hypotheses.description: YieldRegistry.rescue() is callable by any pool admin and forwards arbitrary calldata to YieldAccount.rescue(), which performs a `functionCall` on any target. This allows a pool admin to drain any yield account's funds by calling rescue with a transfer calldata. While pool admin is a trusted role, the function is overly broad and bypasses the account's onlyManager restriction, meaning a compromised or malicious admin can steal user funds. The audit rules exclude trusted roles, but the function's existence combined with the lack of any restriction on target/data makes it a significant centralization risk that could be exploited if admin keys are compromised.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker compromises a pool admin key (or the admin is malicious). 2. Attacker calls `rescue(yieldAccount, token, transferCalldata)` to transfer all tokens from the yield account to the attacker. 3. The YieldAccount.rescue() only checks `msg.sender == yieldRegistry`, which is satisfied.
hypotheses.impact: Complete loss of funds in any yield account.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict rescue to only allow recovering funds to the account owner or a designated safe address, and/or require a timelock/multisig. Consider removing arbitrary calldata execution.

hypotheses.title: YieldStakingBase._unstake allows botAdmin to unstake any NFT without owner consent
hypotheses.description: In `_unstake`, the check `vars.nftOwner == msg.sender || botAdmin == msg.sender` allows the botAdmin to unstake any NFT. The botAdmin is a trusted role set by pool admin, but the function allows the bot to force unstake and set an `unstakeFine` up to `maxUnstakeFine`. The bot can also trigger the unstake without the owner's consent, potentially causing the owner to incur fines or lose yield. While botAdmin is trusted, the ability to force unstake and impose fines on any user is a significant centralization risk.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. A malicious or compromised botAdmin calls `unstake` on a victim's NFT. 2. The bot sets a high `unstakeFine` (up to max). 3. The victim's NFT is unstaked and the fine is deducted from their yield.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of yield/funds for the victim, forced unstaking.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require owner consent for unstaking, or restrict botAdmin to only unstake when health factor is below threshold and cap fines more strictly.

hypotheses.title: YieldStakingBase._repay allows botAdmin to repay on behalf of owner and seize remainAmount
hypotheses.description: In `_repay`, the check `vars.nftOwner == msg.sender || botAdmin == msg.sender` allows the botAdmin to repay a loan. The function transfers `vars.remainAmount` to `vars.nftOwner` (the owner), and `vars.extraAmount` is pulled from `vars.nftOwner`. If the botAdmin calls repay, the extra amount is pulled from the owner's balance, and the remain amount goes to the owner. This is not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor, but the botAdmin can force repayments, potentially causing the owner to pay extra amounts unexpectedly.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Malicious botAdmin calls `repay` on a victim's NFT. 2. If the claimed yield is less than the debt, the contract pulls `extraAmount` from the victim's balance. 3. The victim loses funds without consent.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized fund transfer from victim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require owner consent for repay, or restrict botAdmin to only repay when necessary (e.g., liquidation).
